article.title: Thanksgiving Myth
article.author: Jasmyne Cannick
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I know it's unpopular to talk about certain things on Thanksgiving because apparently we're supposed to suspend our critical thinking for the day in the interest of everybody's comfort. But I'm Gen X, our motto continues to be fuck your feelings, and at my big age, other people's discomfort is not a sufficient reason for me to shut up. If what I'm about to say is going to interfere with your enjoyment of today's festivities, exercise your God-given ability to keep scrolling. I'm not serving dinner, and reading this ain't mandatory. That said… The thing about being a Gen X woman is that the older I get and the more I learn about this country, past and present, the more I find myself questioning some of the shit we grew up doing simply because that’s what everybody else was doing. Thanksgiving is one of those things. We grew up tracing our hands to make turkeys while America conveniently left the stolen land, broken treaties, genocide and forced displacement of Indigenous people out of the lesson plan. Apparently, that part didn’t fit on the bulletin board. America has perfected the art of committing atrocities, rewriting the history, giving itself a federal holiday and throwing in a mattress sale. And please spare me the lecture about Thanksgiving being about gratitude. Gratitude is available 365 days a year, 366 during a leap year. It does not require a federally designated Thursday, a dead bird or a historically questionable origin story. Related: Los Angeles Mayor’s Race: When Progressive Branding Replaces Progressive Governing As a Black woman, I cannot demand that America reckon with what it did to my people while conveniently overlooking what it did to Indigenous people because somebody’s auntie makes exceptional dressing. My commitment to justice is not contingent upon the menu and I’m not about to play intellectually incompetent for the sake of a plate of dressing. My solidarity with other oppressed people shouldn’t go on hiatus because it’s the fourth Thursday in November. And quiet as it’s kept, America is still very much in the business of deciding whose humanity matters and whose doesn’t. Today, so many people will pass human beings splayed across the concrete, sleeping in tents and living on the streets, on their way to somebody’s house to sit around a table and talk about how thankful and blessed they are. Some of those same people will spend tomorrow complaining about the homeless people in their neighborhood. Make that shit make sense. You’re thankful for the roof over your head but resentful of the person who doesn’t have one. Thankful for the food on your table but offended by the person asking for something to eat. But by all means, somebody bless the food. At some point, what we profess to believe has to inform how we actually live. Otherwise, we’re just performing consciousness when it’s convenient. I’m Gen X. I’m old enough to understand that consistency requires sacrifice and that sometimes standing on your principles means sitting out some shit you actually enjoy. Related: The Real Democratic Debate Begins in Los Angeles Listen, I’m not telling anybody what to do with their Thursday. I’m grown and presumably so are you. But I refuse to be more committed to the traditions of my childhood than I am to the convictions of my adulthood. I don’t need a federal holiday to be thankful. I don’t need to participate in America’s historical revisionism to spend time with people I love. And I damn sure don’t need permission from anybody to stop celebrating something that no longer aligns with my beliefs. I can be grateful without celebrating a mythology that sanitizes the suffering of Indigenous people. And I can express that gratitude by giving a damn about the people suffering right outside my door today. Some of us have outgrown Thanksgiving. Not the food. The bullshit. And contrary to popular belief, macaroni and cheese can legally be made any day of the year. Jasmyne's Substack
